Language: Countable nouns form plurals by adding s, es, ies or ves (horse–horses, box–boxes, city–cities, wolf–wolves). Irregular plurals: person–people, man–men, woman–women, child–children, tooth–teeth, foot–feet, mouse–mice, sheep–sheep, deer–deer, fish–fish. Uncountable nouns (water, oil, bread, fruit, love, advice) cannot be counted directly; use amount words: a pound of bread, a glass of water, two litres of oil. Action words in the story: suggested, gathered, failed, waited, managed, caused.

Let's Understand – C1 Answer the following questions in a sentence each (p. 3)
1. Which was the healthiest place that you could imagine?
The earth was the healthiest place one could imagine in olden days.
2. Who was furious?
One of the witches was furious because people were healthy.
3. What made the potion go wrong?
One of the witches made a mistake in uttering the words while the energy was being collected.

They were turned into tiny creatures like germs and trapped in liquid in a small bottle lying in a swamp.
2. What did the boy do with the new drink?

3. How did the boy change after drinking the potion?
He no longer wanted to eat vegetables, fruits and good food. He wanted only pizza, burgers, ice cream and chips, stopped going out to play and became ill.
4. Mention the worst thing that the witches learnt to do.
The witches learnt to jump from one person to another like a virus.

3. What was the advice of Dr. Fitton-Healthy?

Let's Understand – C2 Discuss with your partner and answer the following questions (p. 6)
1. What made people strong and healthy in olden days?
They ate a variety of food, loved fruits and vegetables, took daily exercise and enjoyed walking, running, playing and leaping about.
2. How would the potion change the people?
It would make people lose their desire to eat healthy food and to exercise. They would fall ill, become lazy and lose interest in life.
3. Why were the witches not able to make the kind of magic potion they wanted to prepare?
One of the witches made a mistake in uttering the words while collecting energy, which caused a big explosion.
4. Describe the change in the boy's attitude after he drank the potion.
Earlier he enjoyed vegetables, fruits and play. After drinking the potion he wanted only junk food, stopped going out and became lazy and ill.
5. What was Dr. Fitton-Healthy's best remedy?
To live a healthy, joyful and happy life by eating fruits and vegetables and doing exercise.

C1.1 Name the two characters in the poem.

To remember its exercises: 'Now, don't forget your exercises!'

1. Who invented plastic?
Alexander Parkes created the first man-made plastic.
2. What did he name it?

Check your understanding (p. 23)
1. Why do people dispose plastic everywhere?
Plastic is cheap and easily available, so people throw it away everywhere.
2. Give reasons for plastic pollution.
Plastic is long-lasting, cannot decompose (non-biodegradable), and people dispose of it carelessly after use.
3. Where is plastic pollution seen more?
Plastic pollution is highly concentrated in big cities.
4. Where does the plastic so disposed remain?
It remains in the soil in the same form.
Check your understanding (p. 24)
1. How does plastic cause pollution at every stage of its production?
The chemicals used in making plastic are toxic and damage living beings; and when it is disposed of, it stays in the environment. Even recycling degrades its quality and demands more production.
2. How long can plastic take to decompose?
A single plastic sheet can take about a thousand years to rot.
3. How does it have a bad impact on the earth?
It affects the food chain and is one of the causes of global warming.

lessons.notes: Unit 4 has a prose story 'Leg Trap' (p. 54–61) about the shoeshine boy Dhira, a poem 'Froth and Bubble' by Adam Lindsay Gordon (p. 69–72) and a 'Read and enjoy' poem 'A Bravery Pledge' (p. 72–73). 2. Describe the customer who approached Dhira.

He was afraid that the influential customer might complain to the policemen, so he gave his full attention to the polishing.

Because worldly things are short-lived and unimportant, like froth and bubbles that quickly disappear.

Kindness and courage are strong and lasting, like stone, and they remain firm even when life is uncertain.

lessons.t: Supplementary Reading · The Never Ending Story (ಎಂದೂ ಮುಗಿಯದ ಕಥೆ)
lessons.words: hakim – a physician (ವೈದ್ಯ); durbar – royal court; courtier / durbari – a member of the royal court; huzoor – sir, master; tale – a story; Bhil – a tribal community of central India; pecked – struck with the beak; nibbled – bit off small pieces; disgusted – feeling strong dislike or annoyance
lessons.notes: Supplementary reading (p. 74–77). Birbal tells the Emperor Akbar a never-ending story about a Bhil, birds and grains of corn; the Emperor realises his folly. Teacher note: p. 75 item 9 has the spelling 'happend' – it should be 'happened'. The reading has no separate preparatory activity; only 'Check your understanding' is given.
ab: Check your understanding (p. 77)
1. What did the hakim suggest to the Emperor?
The hakim suggested that the Emperor should hear a story before retiring to bed every night, so that his mind would be cheerful and he could sleep peacefully.
2. Why did the durbaris go to Birbal?
The durbaris could not keep telling stories every night; the Emperor would not sleep, and the storytellers themselves began to feel sleepy.
3. What was Bhil's problem?
The birds entered his hut every day and carried away grains of corn in their beaks.
4. How did Bhil try to solve the problem?
He bought a big basket, kept all the grains of corn in it and closed its lid tightly.
5. What did the little sparrow do?
She made friends with a small mouse in the hut and asked him to help; he nibbled at the basket.
6. Why was the Emperor disgusted?
Birbal's story of the birds going into the hut one by one was dull and endless, with the same 'What next?' again and again.
